source.title: Structure, Dimensionality, and Distribution Shape - What Makes Pretraining Data Transferable, and Why the Input Pipeline Decides Which

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance as synthetic pretraining-corpus size varies in time-series models, a different modality and measure from language-model scaling-loss studies.
record.gate_note: The study reports UCR downstream accuracy as synthetic corpus size changes, which bears on V6. Its experiments do not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling laws, or compute-optimal parameter-token allocation. Calcium replacement and corpus-property results concern transfer, not the power-law loss behavior in V1–V3 or the other untested versions.
record.test_reason: This is a study of which properties of a synthetic corpus make time-series pretraining transfer. It fits no scaling law and varies no model size or compute. It only cites Kaplan and Hoffmann ('data quality known to shift scaling'). Its one size result is that UCR probe accuracy rises with synthetic corpus size for PatchTST. That result has no functional form, so it cannot bear on V5, which needs the power-law form. It is also not a language-model downstream-predictability result, so it does not bear on V6. It is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors' central claim is the Transfer-Invariance Principle: the model's input pipeline, not the data modality, decides which corpus property (structure, dimensionality, distribution shape) governs transfer. Evidence for it: under z-scoring (PatchTST/UCR), structure governs with an interior optimum, and synthetic data matches a real corpus at equal size and exceeds it when scaled. Under unnormalized ΔF/F (POYO+), a shape-matched synthetic corpus replaces real pretraining (0.407 vs 0.386, not significant). Flipping only the normalization changes the shape effect 5.3×. They make no scaling-law claims.
record.recipe_differences: Tests synthetic pretraining-corpus size and downstream classification accuracy in time-series models; does not reproduce language-model cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The input normalization pipeline changes which corpus properties affect transfer. For UCR, the synthetic corpus-size gain is not uniform across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: PatchTST frozen-probe UCR accuracy (22 datasets) rises with synthetic pretraining corpus size. It stays flat near the real-corpus level up to ~4k windows, then rises to 4.2% above it at 16384 windows. KernelSynth rises similarly and ends at the same accuracy. No functional form is fitted and model size is fixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream transfer of time-series foundation models increases with synthetic pretraining-corpus size (data-only scaling of downstream accuracy outside text).

record.code_released: Not stated as a URL; code and configuration files are promised as supplementary material on acceptance.
record.problems: The relevant evidence is time-series downstream accuracy, not language-model held-out loss. The study varies corpus size, not model parameters or training compute, and does not fit a power law or make small-run loss extrapolations. For UCR, the margin is not uniform across datasets; the paper reports 13 of 22 datasets and Wilcoxon p = 0.07. The paper also notes that the normalization flip does not separate distribution shape from per-window scale.
record.rows_left_out: Calcium decoding and other corpus-property experiments were not extracted as rows because they do not test the downstream scale behavior in V6 or the power-law loss claims. The paper's modality table and cited scaling-law findings are not results of language-model scaling experiments.

untested.parts: No held-out LM loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Varies corpus size in time-series models but fits no power law and reports no pretraining loss, so the power-law form in another modality is untested.
No LM downstream performance vs scale or pretraining loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with a V6 'supports' label overreaches. V6 concerns predictable downstream gains in language models, and the study fits no scaling relation. Corpus-size gains are shown on 3 seeds in Figure 2 and are partly generic to any synthetic data, per the authors.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of loss from small language-model runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Architecture-shape effects at a fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes; this paper does not fit or test power laws.
Tests downstream accuracy against synthetic pretraining-corpus size on PatchTST/UCR, not downstream performance against model size or pretraining loss, and not language models.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.note: The synthetic corpus at the same window count as the real corpus is reported as matching the real corpus; paired t-test over seeds, p = 0.60.
rows.check: Time-series PatchTST, not a language model, and no scaling fit. 0.813±0.014 vs 0.805±0.008 no-pretraining is within seed noise, so 'partial' overstates it.

rows.subject: PatchTST
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on synthetic TransferForge corpus; frozen logistic-regression probe
rows.operation_detail: Increased synthetic corpus size at nroots = 4 and compared accuracy with the fixed real corpus.
rows.measure: UCR classification accuracy relative to fixed real-corpus accuracy
rows.note: The paper reports that synthetic accuracy stays at the real-corpus level up to about four thousand windows, then exceeds it.

rows.subject: PatchTST
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on synthetic TransferForge corpus; frozen logistic-regression probe
rows.operation_detail: Compared per-dataset UCR outcomes for the larger synthetic corpus against KernelSynth.
rows.measure: Number of UCR datasets on which TransferForge has the reported margin
rows.value: 1.3% higher on 8 of 10 seeds; margin not uniform across datasets (13 of 22)
rows.uncertainty: paired t-test p = 0.015 over seeds; Wilcoxon p = 0.07 over datasets
rows.note: The average corpus-size gain is not uniform across the 22 evaluation datasets.
rows.check: This compares the study's own generator against KernelSynth at a matched size. It is not a corpus-size effect and should not be framed as scaling. Note that the text says KernelSynth ends at the same accuracy at 16384 windows.
